title: Combining DataFrames with Concatenation, Merge and Join
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of combining dataframes with concatenation, merge and join.
Choose Pandas APIs and parameters that match the input structure.
Apply the operations to deterministic Series and DataFrames.
Validate output shape, schema, data types and missing values.
Recognize edge cases and data-quality risks.

understand.concept: concat stacks objects along an axis, merge performs relational joins on keys, and DataFrame.join is convenient for index-based combination. Join type controls which keys survive. Duplicate keys can multiply rows in many-to-many joins, so validate uniqueness and expected row counts.
understand.whyItMatters: Reliable data workflows ingest, combine, analyze and publish structured information. Correct parsing and transformations prevent silent data loss and misleading conclusions.
understand.analogy: A DataFrame workflow is like organizing labeled records: labels and matching rules determine how records are connected.
understand.summary: concat stacks objects along an axis, merge performs relational joins on keys, and DataFrame.join is convenient for index-based combination. Join type controls which keys survive. Duplicate keys can multiply rows in many-to-many joins, so validate uniqueness and expected row counts.

explain.narrative: This lesson explores combining dataframes with concatenation, merge and join with small reproducible datasets. Inspect input structure before selecting parsing, join, time-frequency or export options. Validate resulting columns, row counts, index, dtypes and missing values. concat stacks objects along an axis, merge performs relational joins on keys, and DataFrame.join is convenient for index-based combination. Join type controls which keys survive. Duplicate keys can multiply rows in many-to-many joins, so validate uniqueness and expected row counts.

examples.title: Concatenate rows
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
a=pd.DataFrame({'id':[1]})
b=pd.DataFrame({'id':[2]})
r=pd.concat([a,b],ignore_index=True)
print(r.id.tolist())
examples.explanation: This deterministic example demonstrates concatenate rows. Compare the output with the expected result and inspect the resulting data structure.

examples.title: Inner merge
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
a=pd.DataFrame({'id':[1,2]})
b=pd.DataFrame({'id':[2,3],'score':[90,80]})
r=a.merge(b,on='id',how='inner')
print(r.to_dict(orient='records'))
examples.explanation: This deterministic example demonstrates inner merge. Compare the output with the expected result and inspect the resulting data structure.

examples.title: Left merge
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
a=pd.DataFrame({'id':[1,2]})
b=pd.DataFrame({'id':[2],'flag':['yes']})
r=a.merge(b,on='id',how='left')
print(r.flag.fillna('missing').tolist())
examples.explanation: This deterministic example demonstrates left merge. Compare the output with the expected result and inspect the resulting data structure.

examples.title: Join by index
examples.explanation: This deterministic example demonstrates join by index. Compare the output with the expected result and inspect the resulting data structure.

examples.title: Validate unique keys
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
a=pd.DataFrame({'id':[1,2]})
b=pd.DataFrame({'id':[1,2],'v':[4,5]})
r=a.merge(b,on='id',validate='one_to_one')
print(len(r))
examples.explanation: This deterministic example demonstrates validate unique keys. Compare the output with the expected result and inspect the resulting data structure.
